claim: Marine mammals are highly sensitive to changes in aquatic ecosystems.
source: Marine mammals are a diverse group of top predators highly sensitive to changes in aquatic ecosystems (Constable et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Constable et al., 2014.

claim: Fur seals and sea lions breed and give birth on land but forage at sea.
source: Within this group, fur seals and sea lions (otariids) breed and give birth on land but forage at sea, alternating periods of foraging in the ocean with periods of offspring attendance and nursing on land (income breeders) (Stephens et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stephens et al., 2009.

claim: Otariids alternate periods of foraging in the ocean with periods of offspring attendance and nursing on land.
source: Within this group, fur seals and sea lions (otariids) breed and give birth on land but forage at sea, alternating periods of foraging in the ocean with periods of offspring attendance and nursing on land (income breeders) (Stephens et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stephens et al., 2009.

claim: Otariids are highly sensitive to local changes in prey distribution and abundance.
source: Therefore, otariids, like other marine mammals, are highly sensitive to local changes in prey distribution and abundance (Trillmich et al., 1991, Constable et al., 2014, Elorriaga-Verplancken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trillmich et al., 1991, Constable et al., 2014, and Elorriaga-Verplancken et al., 2016.

claim: Sea surface temperature is one of the most important indexes of the abundance of marine mammal prey.
source: One of the most important indexes of the abundance of marine mammal prey is sea surface temperature (SST) (Soto et al., 2006, Elorriaga-Verplancken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soto et al., 2006 and Elorriaga-Verplancken et al., 2016.

claim: Warmer SST indicates reduced nutrient upwelling.
source: Warmer SST indicates reduced nutrient upwelling, which is associated with reduced primary productivity and abundance of mesopelagic marine organisms (Lewandowska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lewandowska et al., 2014.

claim: Reduced nutrient upwelling is associated with reduced primary productivity and abundance of mesopelagic marine organisms.
source: Warmer SST indicates reduced nutrient upwelling, which is associated with reduced primary productivity and abundance of mesopelagic marine organisms (Lewandowska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lewandowska et al., 2014.

claim: Decreased food resources force otariid females to increase their foraging trip lengths.
source: This decrease in food resources forces otariid females to change their foraging strategies by increasing their foraging trip lengths, resulting in decreased time spent on land with their pup (maternal attendance) (Trillmich et al., 1991, Costa, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trillmich et al., 1991 and Costa, 2008.

claim: Increased foraging trip lengths result in decreased maternal attendance.
source: This decrease in food resources forces otariid females to change their foraging strategies by increasing their foraging trip lengths, resulting in decreased time spent on land with their pup (maternal attendance) (Trillmich et al., 1991, Costa, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trillmich et al., 1991 and Costa, 2008.

claim: Changes in patterns of maternal attendance have been associated with decreased pup growth.
source: These changes in patterns of maternal attendance have been associated with decreased pup growth and increased mortality (Soto et al., 2006, Jeanniard-du-Dot et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soto et al., 2006 and Jeanniard-du-Dot et al., 2017.

claim: Changes in patterns of maternal attendance have been associated with increased mortality.
source: These changes in patterns of maternal attendance have been associated with decreased pup growth and increased mortality (Soto et al., 2006, Jeanniard-du-Dot et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soto et al., 2006 and Jeanniard-du-Dot et al., 2017.

claim: In some otariid populations, in years with abnormal SST, the immune competence of pups decreases.
source: However, in some otariid populations, in years with abnormal SST, the immune competence of pups decreases (Banuet-Martínez et al., 2017), suggesting that environmental variables can affect the health of marine mammals by impairing their immune function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Banuet-Martínez et al., 2017.

claim: Infectious diseases are one of the most significant causes of mortality among young marine mammals in some populations.
source: In some marine mammal populations, infectious diseases are one of the most significant causes of mortality among young individuals (Gulland and Hall, 2007; Spraker et al., 2007; Seguel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gulland and Hall, 2007; Spraker et al., 2007; and Seguel et al., 2013.

claim: Hookworms (Uncinaria sp.) have been described in nearly all otariid species.
source: In otariids, hookworms (Uncinaria sp.) have been described in nearly all species, and while some populations suffer few adverse effects, others experience up to 70% of hookworm-related mortality being one of the most significant infectious diseases of young fur seals and sea lions (Spraker et al., 2007; Lyons et al., 2011a; Seguel et al., 2013; Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spraker et al., 2007; Lyons et al., 2011a; Seguel et al., 2013; and Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017.

claim: Some otariid populations experience up to 70% hookworm-related mortality.
source: In otariids, hookworms (Uncinaria sp.) have been described in nearly all species, and while some populations suffer few adverse effects, others experience up to 70% of hookworm-related mortality being one of the most significant infectious diseases of young fur seals and sea lions (Spraker et al., 2007; Lyons et al., 2011a; Seguel et al., 2013; Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spraker et al., 2007; Lyons et al., 2011a; Seguel et al., 2013; and Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017.

claim: Fur seals are infected with hookworms during their first 1–4 days of life through their mother's colostrum.
source: Fur seals are infected with hookworms (Uncinaria sp.) during their first 1–4 days of life through their mother's colostrum (Lyons et al., 2011b; Seguel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lyons et al., 2011b and Seguel et al., 2018.

claim: Hookworms live in the small intestine where they bite the mucosa to feed on blood.
source: These nematodes live in the small intestine where they bite the mucosa to feed on blood, causing substantial tissue damage, anemia, and death (Marcus et al., 2015, Seguel et al., 2017, Seguel et al., 2018); however, it is unclear how the host responds to this infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marcus et al., 2015, Seguel et al., 2017, and Seguel et al., 2018.

claim: Hookworms cause substantial tissue damage, anemia, and death in fur seals.
source: These nematodes live in the small intestine where they bite the mucosa to feed on blood, causing substantial tissue damage, anemia, and death (Marcus et al., 2015, Seguel et al., 2017, Seguel et al., 2018); however, it is unclear how the host responds to this infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marcus et al., 2015, Seguel et al., 2017, and Seguel et al., 2018.

claim: Long term studies in fur seal populations show that hookworm prevalence and mortality varies over time.
source: Long term studies in fur seal populations show that hookworm prevalence and mortality varies over time, but the mechanisms driving these patterns are unknown (Lyons et al., 2011a; Seguel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lyons et al., 2011a and Seguel et al., 2013.

claim: The hookworm prepatent period varied from 14 to 18 days.
source: The hookworm (Uncinaria sp.) prepatent period varied from 14 to 18 days and based on the coprological analyses and necropsies of recaptured pups, the number of days a pup released hookworm eggs (infectious period) ranged from 5 to 55 days (2014–15 and 2017, mean = 25.7 ± 10.9, n = 146).
evidence: This is based on coprological analyses and necropsies from the study.

claim: The number of days a pup released hookworm eggs ranged from 5 to 55 days with a mean of 25.7 ± 10.9 days.
source: The hookworm (Uncinaria sp.) prepatent period varied from 14 to 18 days and based on the coprological analyses and necropsies of recaptured pups, the number of days a pup released hookworm eggs (infectious period) ranged from 5 to 55 days (2014–15 and 2017, mean = 25.7 ± 10.9, n = 146).
evidence: This is based on coprological analyses and necropsies from the study.

claim: SAFS females were observed more frequently arriving to the rookery from foraging trips early in the morning.
source: SAFS females were observed more frequently arriving to the rookery from foraging trips early in the morning (2007 = 78/115, 67.8% returning events in the morning, 2017 = 87/135, 64% returning events in the morning).
evidence: This is based on observational data from the study.

claim: Foraging trip length was correlated with the number of nursing events.
source: Foraging trip length was correlated with the number of nursing events, indicating that the more time females spend at sea makes it less likely to observe them nursing their pup (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In 2017, SAFS females spend more time foraging at sea compared to 2007.
source: In 2017, a year with SST above Guafo Island average, SAFS females (n = 21) spend more time foraging at sea compared to 2007 (n = 23), a year with SST below Guafo Island average, therefore in 2017 (n = 79) the level of maternal attendance and pup growth rate were lower than in 2007 (n = 128) (Figure 5B) (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on observational data and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In 2017 the level of maternal attendance was lower than in 2007.
source: In 2017, a year with SST above Guafo Island average, SAFS females (n = 21) spend more time foraging at sea compared to 2007 (n = 23), a year with SST below Guafo Island average, therefore in 2017 (n = 79) the level of maternal attendance and pup growth rate were lower than in 2007 (n = 128) (Figure 5B) (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on observational data and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In 2017 pup growth rate was lower than in 2007.

evidence: This is based on observational data and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In years with high SST, the average concentrations of glucose, cholesterol, parasite-specific IgG, and peripheral blood lymphocytes and basophils were lower than in years with low SST.
source: Between 2012 and 2017 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1), in years with high SST (e.g. 2014), the average concentrations of glucose, cholesterol, parasite-specific IgG, and peripheral blood lymphocytes and basophils were lower than in years with low SST (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on data from 2012-2017 and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The average hookworm infectious period was shorter in years with low SST (GLM, X2 = 6.95, df = 1, p = 0.00036).
source: Similarly, the average hookworm infectious period was shorter in years with low SST (GLM, X2 = 6.95, df = 1, p = 0.00036).
evidence: This is based on GLM statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between mean hookworm burdens of necropsied pups and SST (Linear regression, Ad-R2 = 0.86, p < 0.001).
source: Over a 10-y period (2005–08, 2012–17) (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1 and 2), there was a significant positive correlation between mean hookworm burdens of necropsied pups and SST (Linear regression, Ad-R2 = 0.86, p < 0.001), and between hookworm mortality and SST (Ad-R2 = 0.56, p = 0.016); however, in the case of hookworm prevalence at necropsy the correlation with SST was not significant (Figure 6, supplementary file 9–11) (Ad-R2 = 0.29, p = 0.064).
evidence: This is based on linear regression analysis and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Variations in hookworm disease morbidity and mortality are associated with specific changes in the immune response against the parasite.
source: We showed that variations in hookworm disease morbidity and mortality are associated with specific changes in the immune response against the parasite.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Maternal care was the most important external factor affecting immune response and hookworm clearance.
source: Additionally, maternal care was the most important external factor affecting immune response and hookworm clearance.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Indirect indicators of ocean productivity such as sea surface temperature are correlated with hookworm disease dynamics and overall fur seal pup survival.
source: As otariid maternal care is influenced by ocean environmental conditions and prey availability (Trillmich et al., 1991; Soto et al., 2006; Jeanniard-du-Dot et al., 2017), indirect indicators of ocean productivity such as sea surface temperature are correlated with hookworm disease dynamics and overall fur seal pup survival.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Early hookworm clearance is a unique feature of otariids.
source: Early hookworm clearance is a unique feature of otariids, as all studied natural hookworm infections of land mammals consist of long-term intestinal infections (Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017), suggesting that fur seals have developed efficient mechanisms to clear hookworms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017.

claim: All studied natural hookworm infections of land mammals consist of long-term intestinal infections.
source: Early hookworm clearance is a unique feature of otariids, as all studied natural hookworm infections of land mammals consist of long-term intestinal infections (Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017), suggesting that fur seals have developed efficient mechanisms to clear hookworms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seguel and Gottdenker, 2017.

claim: Parasite clearance in fur seals is mediated mostly by T-lymphocytes, basophils, Th2-type leukocytes, and production of parasite-specific IgG.
source: Based on field experiments and the immune parameters measured in the present study, this parasite clearance process is mediated mostly by T-lymphocytes, basophils, Th2-type leukocytes, and production of parasite-specific IgG.
evidence: This is based on field experiments and immune parameter measurements from the study.

claim: An increase in circulating T-lymphocytes and basophils is associated with hookworm clearance and resistance to re-infection in humans and rodents.
source: These results are similar to changes in peripheral blood leukocytes in humans and rodents infected with hookworms (Loukas and Prociv, 2001; Cortés et al., 2017). In both systems, an increase in circulating T-lymphocytes and basophils is associated with hookworm clearance and resistance to re-infection (Cortés et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Loukas and Prociv, 2001 and Cortés et al., 2017.

claim: The hookworm intestinal brush border contains several digestive and heme-detoxifying enzymes that are crucial for the nematode blood digestion and survival.
source: This anatomical location contains several digestive and heme-detoxifying enzymes that are crucial for the nematode blood digestion and survival (Williamson et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williamson et al., 2003 and Wei et al., 2016.

claim: Hookworm vaccines using digestive enzymes in the nematode intestinal brush border as antigens successfully avoid hookworm development and promote clearance in dogs and humans.
source: A similar mechanism has been experimentally induced in dogs and humans through a hookworm vaccine using the digestive enzymes in the nematode intestinal brush border as antigens (Hotez et al., 2016; Diemert et al., 2017). These vaccines successfully avoid hookworm development and promote clearance (Hotez et al., 2016; Diemert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hotez et al., 2016 and Diemert et al., 2017.

claim: In laboratory rodent models, T-lymphocytes, mast cells, and basophils are important players in the morphological changes of the intestine that facilitate nematode detachment and removal.
source: The morphologic and leukocyte population changes observed in the intestine of pups clearing hookworm infection are similar to those described in laboratory rodent models of hookworm infection. In these systems, T-lymphocytes, mast cells, and basophils are important players in the morphological changes of the intestine that facilitate nematode detachment and removal (Ohnmacht and Voehringer, 2010; Cortés et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohnmacht and Voehringer, 2010 and Cortés et al., 2017.

claim: Fur seal pups infected with hookworms for a shorter period of time were more likely to survive the infection.
source: Fur seal pups infected with hookworms for a shorter period of time were more likely to survive the infection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Pups with higher levels of parasite-specific IgG had shorter hookworm infection.
source: Additionally, pups with higher levels of parasite-specific IgG had shorter hookworm infection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claim: In a wild population of Soay sheep, parasite-specific IgG is the best predictor of survival through the winter.
source: This is similar to what has been found in a wild population of Soay sheep (Ovis aries), where parasite-specific IgG is the best predictor of survival through the winter, precisely when there is scarcity of food resources and likely a more detrimental effect of parasites in the host (Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2016.

claim: In most studied mammal species, IgG production is dependent on T-cell activity and caloric intake, particularly in neonates and children.
source: In most studied mammal species, IgG production is dependent on T-cell activity and caloric intake, particularly in neonates and children (Papier et al., 2014; Ibrahim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Papier et al., 2014 and Ibrahim et al., 2017.

claim: Pups with higher levels of maternal attendance had higher growth rates.
source: As expected, and as reported in other studies in pinnipeds, pups with higher levels of maternal attendance had higher growth rates (Francis et al., 1998; Georges and Guinet, 2000; Arnould and Hindell, 2001a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Francis et al., 1998; Georges and Guinet, 2000; and Arnould and Hindell, 2001a.

claim: In some fur seal species pups can maintain relatively stable glucose levels during fasting.
source: Even though in some fur seal species pups can maintain relatively stable glucose levels during fasting (Arnould and Hindell, 2001a; Verrier et al., 2012), after a couple of days without nursing there is a significant decrease in blood glucose (Arnould et al., 2001b; Champagne et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arnould and Hindell, 2001a and Verrier et al., 2012.

claim: After a couple of days without nursing there is a significant decrease in blood glucose in fur seal pups.
source: Even though in some fur seal species pups can maintain relatively stable glucose levels during fasting (Arnould and Hindell, 2001a; Verrier et al., 2012), after a couple of days without nursing there is a significant decrease in blood glucose (Arnould et al., 2001b; Champagne et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arnould et al., 2001b and Champagne et al., 2012.

claim: Californian sea lion pups with better body condition and higher glucose levels have higher total IgG.
source: For instance, recent studies have shown that Californian sea lion pups with better body condition and higher glucose levels have higher total IgG (Banuet-Martínez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Banuet-Martínez et al., 2017.

claim: In humans and laboratory animals, glucose metabolism is one of the most important factors driving T-cell activity and production of antigen-specific IgG.
source: In humans and laboratory animals, glucose metabolism is one of the most important factors driving T-cell activity and production of antigen-specific IgG (Mohammed et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2012 and Palmer et al., 2015.

claim: Fur seal and sea lion maternal attendance patterns can be affected by prey availability, maternal experience, and body condition.
source: Fur seal and sea lion maternal attendance patterns can be affected by several factors, including prey availability, maternal experience, and body condition (Georges and Guinet, 2000; Arnould and Hindell, 2001a; Soto et al., 2006; McDonald et al., 2012a; McDonald et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Georges and Guinet, 2000; Arnould and Hindell, 2001a; Soto et al., 2006; McDonald et al., 2012a; and McDonald et al., 2012b.

claim: Body condition and prey availability can be affected by changes in sea surface temperatures.
source: Out of these variables, body condition and prey availability can be affected by changes in sea surface temperatures (SST) because of the role that ocean temperature plays in nutrient upwelling, primary productivity, and distribution of fish stocks (Soto et al., 2006, Costa, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soto et al., 2006 and Costa, 2008.

claim: In the southern Pacific Ocean, warmer ocean temperature is associated with a marked decrease in primary productivity and fish stocks.
source: In the southern Pacific Ocean, warmer ocean temperature is associated with a marked decrease in primary productivity and fish stocks, these effects being particularly intense during El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events (Trillmich et al., 1991; Soto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trillmich et al., 1991 and Soto et al., 2006.

claim: In 'El Nino' years, the isotopic signature of pup tissues changes, which suggest shifts in the foraging and attendance regimes of their mothers.
source: Additionally, in 'El Nino' years, the isotopic signature of pup tissues changes, which suggest shifts in the foraging and attendance regimes of their mothers (Elorriaga-Verplancken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Elorriaga-Verplancken et al., 2016.

claim: When environmental variation affects prey resources, adult females will increase their foraging intensity effort and metabolic rate before increasing foraging trip length.
source: This model suggests that when environmental variation affects prey resources, adult females will increase their foraging intensity effort and metabolic rate before increasing foraging trip length, because the latter almost always results in a decrease in the net energy delivered to the offspring (Costa, 2008; Costa, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Costa, 2008 and Costa, 2012.

claim: Increasing foraging trip length almost always results in a decrease in the net energy delivered to the offspring.
source: This model suggests that when environmental variation affects prey resources, adult females will increase their foraging intensity effort and metabolic rate before increasing foraging trip length, because the latter almost always results in a decrease in the net energy delivered to the offspring (Costa, 2008; Costa, 2012).

claim: Long-term studies on hookworm infection of fur seals have found dramatic changes in hookworm prevalence and mortality over a 20–30-year period.
source: Similar long-term studies on hookworm infection of fur seals have found dramatic changes in hookworm prevalence and mortality over a 20–30-y period (Lyons et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lyons et al., 2011b.

claim: The Guafo Island fur seal population has remained stable over the last decade.
source: Our observations could explain why changes in prevalence and its correlation to environmental variables were not significant in our study, as the Guafo Island population has remained stable over the last decade (Pavés et al., 2016).

claim: Global climate change is increasing ocean temperature, particularly in the Southern Hemisphere.
source: Global climate change is increasing ocean temperature, particularly in the Southern Hemisphere (Wijffels et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wijffels et al., 2016.

claim: Under climate change scenarios, infectious diseases could have a more detrimental impact on populations of fur seals and sea lions in the future.
source: Our findings highlight that under this scenario infectious diseases could have a more detrimental impact on populations of fur seals and sea lions in the future, but also provide a foundation for the study of climate change adaptation options for these species (Hobday et al., 2015).
